# Agentic Failure Taxonomy {#sec-vol3-app-failure-taxonomy}

An agent that fails rarely crashes. It keeps calling tools that return success, reports a finished task in fluent prose, and leaves the evidence of what went wrong spread across its context, its log, and the environment it touched, which is the fail-plausible fault model of @sec-vol3-intro-fail-plausible seen in production. This appendix classifies the recurring failure modes of agent systems by the symptoms an engineer can observe, the H·S·A exposure each one stresses, the principle it violates, and the mechanism in the main text that closes it, so that a reader facing an anomaly can name it, find the component that should have caught it, and turn it into a regression task.

## How to Use This Appendix {.unnumbered}

Start from what you observe, not from what you suspect.

- **When an agent keeps calling valid tools, every call succeeds, and the task does not advance**, see @sec-vol3-fail-semantic-livelocks.
- **When cost and latency per turn climb and the agent begins ignoring constraints stated early in the task**, see @sec-vol3-fail-context-saturation.
- **When a reward, pass rate, or selector score rises while the work it measures does not improve**, see @sec-vol3-fail-goodhart-collapse.
- **When an agent takes an action nobody asked for after reading untrusted content, or sends data somewhere it should not**, see @sec-vol3-fail-confused-deputy.
- **When several agents or samples agree confidently on a wrong answer**, see @sec-vol3-fail-correlated-consensus.
- **When the agent acts on files, records, or results that no longer exist or have already changed**, see @sec-vol3-fail-environmental-desync.
- **When a trajectory loses its progress after a crash, or repeats an effect after it resumes**, see @sec-vol3-fail-lost-progress.
- **When one failing dependency drains budgets across many trajectories**, see @sec-vol3-fail-retry-storm.
- **For a side-by-side comparison of all eight modes**, see @tbl-vol3-failure-taxonomy-matrix, and **for a step-by-step incident procedure**, see @sec-vol3-fail-diagnostic-checklist.

## Failure Taxonomy Matrix {#sec-vol3-fail-matrix}

@Tbl-vol3-failure-taxonomy-matrix places each failure mode by the exposure it stresses and the principle it violates. The exposure column says which part of the runtime should have closed the failure, and the principle column says which invariant was not enforced. A failure whose closure is missing is a runtime defect, to be fixed at rungs 1 to 3 of the intervention ladder (@sec-vol3-conclusion-adaptation); only a failure that persists with its closure in place is a candidate for training.

| Failure mode                           | Exposure                      | Principle violated                     | Observable signature                                                            | Primary cause                                                                        | Closing mechanism                                                                                                               |
|:---------------------------------------|:------------------------------|:---------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **No-progress loop**                   | Horizon                       | \ref{pri-vol3-preemptive-interrupts}   | Activity and spending rise without established task progress                    | Supervision relies on activity or model reports rather than scoped progress evidence | Budgets and progress detection (@sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting, @sec-vol3-sagas-watchdogs)                                   |
| **Context overflow and dilution**      | State ($S_1$)                 | \ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}   | Cost per turn climbs; early constraints ignored; malformed tool calls           | An append-only context with no budget, compaction, or invalidation                   | Context budget, compaction, and staging (@sec-vol3-context-engineering)                                                         |
| **Reward hacking and verifier gaming** | None (training and selection) | \ref{pri-vol3-verifiable-rewards}      | Score rises while the task outcome does not; tests edited or bypassed           | A verifier the policy can reach, or one that checks less than the task requires      | Isolated, sealed verifiers (@sec-vol3-rlvr-sandboxing, @sec-vol3-evaluation-gyms)                                               |
| **Confused deputy and injection**      | Authority                     | \ref{pri-vol3-zero-trust-sandboxing}   | Unrequested privileged calls after reading untrusted text; unexpected egress    | Untrusted content steering an agent that holds authority and a way out               | Capabilities, egress control, taint tracking, approval gates (@sec-vol3-sandboxes)                                              |
| **Correlated agreement**               | All three, multiplied         | \ref{pri-invariant-closure}            | Unanimous votes or debate consensus on a wrong answer                           | Samples and agents that share a model share its blind spots                          | A deterministic gate commits, not a vote (@sec-vol3-multiagent-consensus)                                                       |
| **Environment desynchronization**      | State ($S_2$, $S_3$)          | \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}        | Actions on files or records that changed; conflicting edits; duplicated creates | Context or index copies trusted over their source; concurrent writers                | Invalidation, version checks, workspace isolation (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot, @sec-vol3-multiagent-concurrency) |
| **Lost progress and repeated effects** | Horizon                       | \ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}    | Restart from the beginning after a crash; an effect applied twice on resume     | Progress held only in memory; effects dispatched before their intent was durable     | Trajectory log, write-ahead intent, settlement (@sec-vol3-durable-execution)                                                    |
| **Retry storm**                        | Authority and Horizon         | \ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement} | One dependency's failures multiply across trajectories; budgets drain           | Retries, overlapping work, or synchronized arrivals amplify dependency load          | Circuit breaker with a typed observation (@sec-vol3-sagas-containment)                                                          |

: **Taxonomy of Agentic Failure Modes**: Eight recurring failure modes, the H·S·A exposure each stresses, the principle it violates, how it shows itself, its primary cause, and the mechanism in the main text that closes it. {#tbl-vol3-failure-taxonomy-matrix tbl-colwidths="[14,11,12,21,21,21]"}

## No-Progress Loops {#sec-vol3-fail-semantic-livelocks}

A *no-progress loop* is a trajectory that continues activity without demonstrated task progress. Calls may complete, fail, or repeat while candidate state and check evidence show no useful advance. A responsive process can still be stuck, and a stalled task need not lose every heartbeat. Progress supervision therefore needs task-scoped evidence as well as liveness and resource signals (principle \ref{pri-vol3-preemptive-interrupts}).

### Observable symptoms

1. **Spend without change.** Turns, tokens, and dollars rise while the environment (the diff, the test results, the database records) stays the same or alternates between two states.
2. **Action flapping.** The agent applies an edit, sees a different failure, reverts the edit, sees the original failure, and applies the edit again. @Sec-vol3-sagas-watchdogs opens on this pattern.
3. **Activity without progress.** Tool calls may exit cleanly and model calls may return promptly even when the task is stuck. Health checks alone can miss this condition.
4. **Rising cumulative input cost.** Under an append-only, no-reuse workload with fixed per-turn growth, cumulative input processing grows quadratically; other context and serving policies change this cost (@sec-vol3-sagas-watchdogs).

### Causes

Supervision cannot rely on activity or model reports alone. Useful diagnosis can leave the workspace unchanged, while irrelevant edits can disguise repetition. Missing candidate versions or check conditions make comparisons unreliable. Compaction can omit relevant failure evidence, and uninformative tool observations can leave the next proposal without a useful diagnosis (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction, @sec-vol3-tool-calling-observation-parsing).

### Closing mechanisms

1. **Budgets as the backstop.** Enforced admission limits stop further work without relying on the model to recognize a loop. Account for actual consumption, reserved liability, and the deadline; a stop does not settle outstanding effects or erase incurred charges (@sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting).
2. **Assess possible nonprogress.** Compare task-relevant state, actions, and check evidence under their recorded revisions and conditions. Equal observed hashes can accompany useful waiting or inspection, and changed state can still be useless. Account for detector false positives, missed cycles, and monitoring cost (@sec-vol3-sagas-watchdogs). A ranking-function proof requires separate assumptions; it is not supplied by hash equality.
3. **Preserve relevant failure evidence.** Retain the evidence and dependencies needed for the next decision. The bounded observation and durable record have distinct capture and retention contracts (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction, @sec-vol3-persistence-replay).
4. **Choose a bounded response.** A warning, further investigation, a revised proposal, compatible backtracking, compensation, or escalation can be appropriate. Current effect evidence, authority, and resource limits decide what is admissible. A warning or temperature change does not guarantee progress (@sec-vol3-sagas-forward-vs-backward).

## Context Overflow and Dilution {#sec-vol3-fail-context-saturation}

*Context overflow* is the failure of a trajectory whose context has outgrown what the model can use. It has two halves. The cost half is mechanical. Every call re-sends the whole context, so a context that grows by $\Delta$ tokens per turn from an initial $L_0$ re-sends $T L_0 + T(T-1)\Delta/2$ tokens over $T$ turns, and the time to the first output token grows with the input (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-physics). The quality half is statistical. Models retrieve and combine evidence placed in the middle of a long context less reliably than evidence at its ends, so the usable context is shorter than the nominal window (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-physics).

### Observable symptoms

1. **Cost and latency per turn climb.** Input tokens per call rise turn over turn, and the prefix-cache hit rate falls if anything near the top of the context changes.
2. **Early constraints are ignored.** The agent follows the most recent tool output and the system prompt but violates a constraint stated in an earlier turn, such as a forbidden path.
3. **Tool calls degrade.** Arguments go missing or take the wrong type as tool definitions and parameter descriptions compete with large observations for the model's attention.
4. **Serving memory pressure.** Long-lived trajectories hold large attention state, and fewer of them fit on a server at once (@sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry).

### Causes

The context is treated as an append-only transcript. A shell command that dumps a ten-thousand-line build log, a file read that returns a whole module, or a web page with its markup intact enters the context in full and stays there for the rest of the trajectory, paid for on every turn and diluting the evidence that matters.

### Closing mechanisms

1. **A budget, allocated.** The context budget divides a working set among the system prompt, tool definitions, task, history, retrieved evidence, and output reserve (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-physics; principle \ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}).
2. **Shaping at the source.** Long tool output is truncated, paginated, or reduced to a structured result before it enters the context, with markers that say what was cut (@sec-vol3-tool-calling-streaming).
3. **Compaction and progress notes.** Old tool results are shortened while preserving the exact fields needed by the current task and access to retained originals where available. Structured progress notes carry constraints, version-scoped observations, and unresolved work into the next request; they do not establish durable execution recovery (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction, @sec-vol3-context-engineering-summarization).
4. **Retrieve instead of retain.** Material the agent may need later belongs in a store it can search, not in the context it re-sends (@sec-vol3-long-term-memory-agentic-retrieval).
5. **Serving-side relief.** When the pressure is memory rather than quality, the serving layer evicts, recomputes, or offloads attention state during tool waits and shares prefixes across branches (@sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping, @sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention).

## Reward Hacking and Verifier Gaming {#sec-vol3-fail-goodhart-collapse}

*Reward hacking* is a policy raising its measured reward through behavior that does not accomplish the task the reward was meant to measure (@sec-vol3-rlvr-pathologies). The same failure can appear without training when candidate search exploits gaps in its selector's score. Increasing the search budget creates more opportunities to encounter such candidates, but the selected output's error rate depends on the candidate distribution and selection policy (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-verification). Both are Goodhart's law applied to a verifier [@goodhart1984].

### Observable symptoms

1. **Score and outcome diverge.** Training reward or best-of-$n$ selection scores rise while held-out evaluation on sealed tests stays flat or falls.
2. **Tests edited or bypassed.** Candidate diffs modify test files, weaken assertions, skip tests, or special-case the test inputs.
3. **Grader probing.** Trajectories read the grading scripts, the test runner's configuration, or its environment before producing a solution.
4. **Degenerate outputs under learned rewards.** Where a learned reward model or judge supplies the reward, outputs drift toward the patterns it scores highly, such as length or confident phrasing, rather than toward correctness.

### Causes

The verifier is reachable or incomplete. A verifier that runs where the policy can write, or whose tests live in the policy's workspace, can be satisfied by changing the verifier. A verifier that checks less than the task requires, such as a test suite that never exercises the failure being fixed, can be satisfied by work that does not do the task. Learned verifiers add a third cause, because they have their own errors that optimization finds (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}).

### Closing mechanisms

1. **Isolate the verifier.** Protect evaluation logic, evidence, and credentials from both the agent process and untrusted submitted artifacts. Execute candidate code under the grader's stated isolation and observation contract (@sec-vol3-rlvr-sandboxing, @sec-vol3-evaluation-gyms).
2. **Protect acceptance checks.** Enforce the patch-admission policy for designated grading artifacts. A task can legitimately modify development tests without granting permission to weaken its independent acceptance checks (@sec-vol3-verifier-gaming).
3. **Match the grader to the criterion.** Use mechanical checks for the properties they cover and calibrated judgment where the declared rubric requires it. A judge cannot override a failed mandatory check; favorable agreement does not establish truth (@sec-vol3-evaluation-grading). Training admission applies its separate learning-use criteria (@sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-rankers).
4. **Watch the gap.** Track sealed held-out performance alongside training reward, and treat a widening gap as a verifier defect to fix before training continues (@sec-vol3-rlvr-pathologies).

## Confused Deputy Attacks and Prompt Injection {#sec-vol3-fail-confused-deputy}

A *confused deputy* uses its authority on behalf of a requester whose scope does not justify that use. For an agent, third-party text can steer a proposal through indirect prompt injection (@sec-vol3-security-threat-model). The disclosure path in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-threat-model combines private-data access, attacker-influenced behavior, and an outbound channel. Other harmful effects, such as a destructive local edit, need not use that same path.

### Observable symptoms

1. **Unrequested privileged calls.** An agent summarizing an email or triaging an issue calls a tool that writes, sends, or deletes, and nothing in the task asked for it.
2. **Unauthorized disclosure.** An outbound request carries information the task may not send to its recipient. The destination may be an approved service while the query, headers, or body contain private data that service may not receive.
3. **Borrowed voices in the reasoning.** The trajectory cites instructions that no operator gave, such as a claimed override embedded in retrieved text.
4. **Cross-tenant access.** An agent acting for one tenant reads or changes another tenant's data after ingesting content from a shared resource.

### Causes

Instruction hierarchy and source framing help distinguish task instructions from observations, but they do not enforce resource authority. An attacker can try to redirect a proposal through permitted interfaces. Damage need not require a stolen credential or a forbidden tool: an otherwise permitted search can transmit confidential task data unless the runtime checks the information and its recipient.

### Closing mechanisms

1. **Label provenance in the context.** Untrusted text is staged in marked zones with its source, which lowers the probability that the model treats it as instruction (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging; @sec-vol3-persistent-quarantine for retrieved content).
2. **Grant only what the task needs.** A capability names the rights, objects, argument bounds, and expiry of each grant, and attenuates as work is delegated, so a steered proposal can reach only what the task could (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-least-privilege, @sec-vol3-multiagent-authority).
3. **Broker selected credentials.** Keep those credentials outside the guest and mediate their task-scoped use. Repository contents and returned observations can still contain sensitive data (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-credential-brokering).
4. **Govern outbound paths.** Enforce permitted routes, destinations, and supported operation limits, including applicable name-resolution and local-service access. Permitted request bodies can still disclose information, requiring the information-flow policy developed in Security (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-network, @sec-vol3-security-exfiltration).
5. **Enforce information-flow policy.** Retain runtime-owned integrity provenance and confidentiality metadata through derived values and handles. Check the requested use and destination before dispatch. Reader extraction narrows raw exposure without making its fields trusted or public (@sec-vol3-security-taint-tracking; @sec-vol3-security-quarantined-readers).
6. **Hold calls requiring approval.** Policy-selected calls remain undispatched while authorization is pending. Before dispatch, verify the approved scope, current grants, budget, and applicable action-time conditions (@sec-vol3-controlplane-hitl).

Model-visible source labels support interpretation; host-owned provenance records support enforcement when adapters preserve their dependencies and the runtime checks the actual operation. Capabilities, brokering, egress policy, information-flow checks, and applicable approval gates address different paths. Their protection depends on the resources and channels they cover, not on the model's description of its intentions.

## Correlated Agreement {#sec-vol3-fail-correlated-consensus}

*Correlated agreement* is the failure of a voting ensemble, a self-consistency vote, or a multi-agent debate that converges confidently on a wrong answer. It undermines the intuition that more independent opinions make a decision safer, because samples and agents built on the same model, or on models trained on overlapping data, are not independent.

### Observable symptoms

1. **Unanimous and wrong.** Every sample or agent produces the same incorrect patch or answer, often with high stated confidence.
2. **Herding in debate.** A later agent adopts an earlier agent's claim instead of defending its own correct reasoning, and the discussion converges on the first answer stated.
3. **Agreement mistaken for evidence.** An agreement score of 1.0 clears a review threshold that was meant to catch uncertain results.
4. **Plausible shared errors.** The wrong answer is not malformed. It is a subtle misreading of the specification or an assumed interface that every participant shares.

### Causes

Majority voting helps only as far as errors are independent. When a fraction of tasks falls into a blind spot that every voter shares, no number of voters recovers those tasks, and the ensemble's accuracy is bounded by one minus that fraction (@sec-vol3-appendix-math-correlated-quorum). Debate adds a second cause, since each agent reads the others' text and is conditioned by it.

### Closing mechanisms

1. **Commit through an invariant gate, not a vote.** Generate and rank candidates with as much diversity as is affordable, but let a deterministic check that no agent can modify decide what is committed (@sec-vol3-multiagent-consensus; principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}).
2. **Diversify what can be diversified.** Different model families, prompts, and decompositions reduce the shared fraction, by an amount that must be measured on the task, but do not remove it.
3. **Do not let critics grade by confidence.** In debate, a critic that reads a confident, well-formed answer tends to adopt it, so critique adds influence rather than independent evidence unless the critic checks the answer against the task (@sec-vol3-multiagent-consensus).
4. **Select with evidence relevant to the task.** An executable check can distinguish candidates that agreement alone cannot, but its value depends on coverage, error rates, and cost. Compare the selected output under the task's evidence standard rather than treating either a passing check or a majority vote as conclusive (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-candidate-diversity).

---

## Environment Desynchronization {#sec-vol3-fail-environmental-desync}

*Environment desynchronization* is the failure of an agent whose picture of the environment, carried in its context, its retrieval indexes, or its memory, no longer matches the environment itself. The agent then acts correctly on a world that no longer exists.

### Observable symptoms

1. **Acting on ghosts.** The agent reads, edits, or deletes a path that an earlier turn moved or removed, relying on a directory listing still in its context.
2. **Redundant creation.** The agent creates a branch, table, or file that already exists and derails on the error.
3. **Retrieval that contradicts the tools.** A search returns the old version of code the agent just edited, and the agent concludes its edit failed and applies it again (@sec-vol3-persistent-need).
4. **Conflicting writers.** Two agents working in the same workspace overwrite each other's edits and produce failures neither can reproduce alone.
5. **Late results.** A tool result arrives after its deadline and is taken as the answer to a later call.

### Causes

A copy is trusted over its source. Observations in the context, entries in a retrieval index, and notes in agent-written memory are all derived from the environment at some moment, and nothing ties them to the source's later changes unless the runtime does (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}). Shared workspaces without isolation, and tool calls retried without settlement, add changes the agent did not observe.

### Closing mechanisms

1. **Invalidate affected current-state observations.** Bind each staged observation to its dependencies and reconsider its current use when a relevant source changes. Historical observations may remain with their original scope (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot).
2. **Check derived copies against the source.** Current-state candidates must satisfy the retrieval contract's applicable source generation and provenance requirements. Excluding an obsolete index entry does not supply a current replacement; the result may require an authorized source read or an explicit partial or unavailable status (@sec-vol3-persistent-governance, @sec-vol3-persistent-invalidation).
3. **Check versions on write.** An edit carries the version hash of the file it read, and a mismatch fails the edit with a structured observation that tells the model to re-read (@sec-vol3-multiagent-concurrency).
4. **Isolate workspaces.** Give each trajectory, and each concurrent agent, its own leased workspace, merged back through a verification gate (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-lease, @sec-vol3-multiagent-concurrency).
5. **Preserve settlement evidence.** Retain the operation identity and endpoint repeat contract after an ambiguous timeout (@sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency). Reject direct append to an obsolete continuation, but authenticate and correlate late evidence with the unresolved operation (@sec-vol3-controlplane-statemachine).

---

## Lost Progress and Repeated Effects {#sec-vol3-fail-lost-progress}

*Lost progress* is the failure of a long trajectory that cannot survive the loss of the process running it. Its twin, the *repeated effect*, appears when a naive restart does survive, by replaying from memory or asking the model again, and dispatches an effect that had already happened.

### Observable symptoms

1. **Restart from the beginning.** After a worker crash, a deployment, or a preemption, the trajectory starts over, repeating minutes or hours of model calls.
2. **Duplicate external effects.** A resumed trajectory sends a second email, opens a second pull request, or charges twice.
3. **Resumed trajectories that behave differently.** Re-invoking the model may produce different proposals; it does not reconstruct the recorded execution (@sec-vol3-persistence-non-determinism).
4. **Approvals that vanish.** A trajectory paused for approval is lost when its host restarts, and the approval arrives for a trajectory that no longer exists.

### Causes

Progress lives only in memory, or effects leave the host before the record that authorizes them is durable. In the first case nothing survives the crash. In the second, the log cannot say whether an effect happened, and a retry on the assumption that it did not is how duplicates occur (principle \ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}).

### Closing mechanisms

1. **Reconstruct from available authoritative history.** Preserve typed decisions and evidence under a stated storage failure domain. A fixed reducer and required available artifacts rebuild the selected record (@sec-vol3-persistence-event-sourcing).
2. **Acknowledge intent before dispatch.** The acknowledgment must survive the declared failures. Absence of intent establishes no dispatch only in a complete surviving authoritative history under the enforced barrier contract (@sec-vol3-persistence-wal).
3. **Reconcile what is in doubt.** On resume, an intent without adequate terminal outcome evidence requires the endpoint's supported result-recovery contract or adequate reconciliation evidence. A key or unchanged-state probe alone cannot exclude a delayed effect. Preserve unresolved status and escalate when safe repetition cannot be established (@sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency, @sec-vol3-persistence-migration).
4. **Publish compatible checkpoints.** Bind record, workspace, and required artifacts to an exact log boundary after durable availability; reconstruct the affected state through the suffix. Compare checkpoint cost with recorded-event and workspace reconstruction cost under the workload and failure assumptions (@sec-vol3-persistence-checkpointing).
5. **Separate reconstruction from new execution.** Fold recorded decisions without regenerating past model outputs. For harness regression replay, supply the captured inputs required at the chosen boundary and disable live effects; missing capture limits the test (@sec-vol3-persistence-replay).

---

## Retry Storms {#sec-vol3-fail-retry-storm}

A *retry storm* occurs when retries amplify load on a failing dependency. Repeated proposals, client-library retries, overlapping remote work, or synchronized arrivals can extend an outage and consume many trajectories' allowances. A slowdown does not itself imply amplification: a fixed population of sequential clients can instead submit fewer requests while waiting longer.

### Observable symptoms

1. **Correlated budget exhaustion.** Many trajectories that share a dependency end on budget ceilings within the same window.
2. **Rephrased retries.** Successive calls to the failing tool differ only in wording or argument order, because the model treats a service failure as a problem with its query.
3. **Load that prevents recovery.** Request rates to the failing service rise after it starts failing.

### Causes

Retry ownership can be fragmented across the model-directed continuation, client libraries, and gateways. Independent allowances at those layers multiply attempts. Timeouts can also leave earlier remote work active when another attempt begins. Correlated failures synchronize retries unless timing and actual admission are controlled. The model is one possible source of repetition, not its only cause.

### Closing mechanisms

1. **Gate dependency load.** Scope a breaker to the dependency, operation, and tenant evidence its policy measures. Open state withholds new admissions; bounded current-generation probes test recovery without bypassing other guards (@sec-vol3-sagas-containment).
2. **Report withheld work accurately.** A typed refusal identifies the withheld proposal and the applicable retry or cooldown guidance. It does not change the status of earlier in-flight operations or force the model to cooperate (@sec-vol3-sagas-containment).
3. **Establish safe repetition or retain uncertainty.** A mutating call that timed out is not simply resent. Use its supported repeat contract and available evidence; unresolved effects may require withholding the retry (@sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency; principle \ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}).
4. **Bound retained work and select a permitted alternative.** Coordinate retry ownership across layers and bound execution, queues, and outstanding remote obligations. Jitter changes arrival timing, not a guaranteed peak. An alternative tool, model, or bounded wait still requires current authority, deadline, budget, and unresolved-operation guards (@sec-vol3-sagas-containment, @sec-vol3-sagas-forward-vs-backward).

## Incident Triage Workflow {#sec-vol3-fail-diagnostic-checklist}

When an agent system degrades, preserve evidence and apply necessary containment while investigating. @Tbl-vol3-triage-workflow supplies a diagnostic checklist, not a universally ordered or guaranteed attribution procedure. A replay requires adequate captured inputs; missing replay coverage does not rule out other useful evidence. @Sec-vol3-evaluation-postmortems develops the limits of replay and controlled comparisons.

|  Step | Phase                   | Diagnostic action                                                                                                         | Failure modes it separates                                                                                    | Evidence it produces                                                                                                          |
|:-----:|:------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **1** | **Secure the evidence** | Retain available evidence; hold model-directed admission while preserving narrowly authorized cleanup                     | All                                                                                                           | Capture gaps, enforced holds, unresolved duties, and current owners (@sec-vol3-sagas-quarantine)                              |
| **2** | **Check the boundary**  | Compare granted capabilities, egress, and tainted inputs with the calls actually made                                     | Confused deputy (@sec-vol3-fail-confused-deputy)                                                              | Capability and egress records; taint marks on arguments                                                                       |
| **3** | **Check progress**      | Look for repeated action hashes, unchanged environment state, and budget burn without state change                        | No-progress loop (@sec-vol3-fail-semantic-livelocks), retry storm (@sec-vol3-fail-retry-storm)                | Progress signals and per-dependency failure rates                                                                             |
| **4** | **Check the context**   | Measure input tokens per turn, cache-hit rate, and where the violated constraint sat in the context                       | Context overflow (@sec-vol3-fail-context-saturation)                                                          | Per-turn token accounting from the trace                                                                                      |
| **5** | **Check the world**     | Compare what the context and indexes said with the source; look for late results and concurrent writers                   | Environment desynchronization (@sec-vol3-fail-environmental-desync)                                           | Version mismatches, late outcome evidence and continuation eligibility, write conflicts                                       |
| **6** | **Check durability**    | Check durable admission evidence; distinguish adequate outcome evidence from unresolved operations                        | Lost progress and repeated effects (@sec-vol3-fail-lost-progress)                                             | Unresolved intents; correlated endpoint effects and attempts                                                                  |
| **7** | **Check the verifiers** | Inspect grader protection, submitted-code execution, criterion coverage, and independent assessment                       | Reward hacking (@sec-vol3-fail-goodhart-collapse), correlated agreement (@sec-vol3-fail-correlated-consensus) | Grader versions and coverage; assessment disagreements and held-out results                                                   |
| **8** | **Test explanations**   | Reconstruct available history; replay captured inputs where supported; run controlled interventions under stated fixtures | Potential model, harness, and environment contributions                                                       | Scoped comparative evidence, competing explanations, capture limits, and a regression case (@sec-vol3-evaluation-postmortems) |

: **Incident Triage Workflow**: A diagnostic checklist that preserves evidence and supports tested explanations and scoped regression checks. Investigations can revisit or combine its phases. {#tbl-vol3-triage-workflow tbl-colwidths="[6,14,32,24,24]"}

Evidence for a harness or environment defect directs a repair there, with tests of the affected postconditions. Persistent policy-related failures can motivate considering training, but attribution can remain mixed or uncertain. Curation decides whether that evidence and the candidate trajectories support a training intervention (@sec-vol3-flywheel-gap).
